intro: Zalgiriai maps one tree, standing at the end of a trail with a strange claim to fame: the writer it is named for watched local peat-cutters at work here and turned their lives into a novella, which F.W. Murnau filmed in 1927 as Sunrise, winning three awards at the first Academy Awards. The oak is the only natural monument in Nemunas Delta Regional Park, three trunks from one base at a combined girth of 4.62 metres. Nobody has dated it: a combined multi-trunk measurement makes the usual growth-rate arithmetic unreliable, so this page asks rather than guesses.

question_answer: The tree mapped at Zalgiriai is the Hermann Sudermann Oak, a three-trunked pedunculate oak at the end of the Zalgiriai heritage trail, the sole natural monument in Nemunas Delta Regional Park. It is named for the writer whose novella about the local peat-cutters became F.W. Murnau's 1927 film Sunrise.

The colony he wrote about is gone and the cutting has stopped, and the trail now runs through what those workers left behind. Nobody has dated the oak: the girth is a combined figure for three trunks rather than one stem, which makes the usual growth-rate arithmetic unreliable, so the age stays an open question.

trees.story:
Three Academy Awards trace back to the bog at the end of this trail. Hermann Sudermann, the German-language writer the oak is named for, stayed often in the village of Zalgiriai and watched the peat-cutters at work here, then wrote their lives into his novella Die Reise nach Tilsit. F.W. Murnau filmed it in 1927 as Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans, which took three awards at the first Academy Awards ceremony. The tree stands at the far end of the roughly two kilometre trail through that former peat-cutters' colony, and it is the reason for the walk rather than a stop along the way.

It is also the only natural monument in the whole of Nemunas Delta Regional Park. Three trunks rise from one base, 4.62 metres round between them and 17.6 metres tall. Lithuania placed it under state protection in 2005.

Sudermann died in 1928, a year after the film. The colony he wrote about is gone and the cutting has stopped, and the trail now runs through what those workers left behind. The oak is the last thing on it.

Nobody has dated this one. The recorded girth is a combined figure for three trunks rather than a single stem, which makes the usual growth-rate arithmetic unreliable, so the age stays an open question. If you know it, tell us.
